narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. The strongest influence came from your third-year grades, which placed you in the second decile of your class. This is well below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted, and it strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.60 was the second most important factor; because it sits noticeably above the 3.23 average of accepted students, it worked in your favor and pulled the prediction back toward passing. The third key factor was your LSAT score of 27, which is substantially lower than the 37 average among accepted applicants and therefore pushed the outcome back toward failure, though with less force than your third-year class ranking.

Taken together, the model saw your recent academic performance in law school and your LSAT result as outweighing the positive signal from your strong undergraduate record.

You should focus on improving your class rank in the remaining years and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. These two steps would most directly address the factors that led to the rejection.
